blocks.text: Chapter 6.
Execute, Monitor, and Judge the Process — Not the Outcome
Sixth night, friend — and it opens high on Everest, in the thin blue air above eight thousand meters.

Experienced climbers make one decision before leaving camp that decides everything: the turnaround time — the exact hour at which they will turn back, regardless of how close the summit looks. Why decide in the valley what you'll do on the ridge? Because the moment of temptation is the worst possible moment to weigh the choice, friend: at altitude, oxygen-starved, years of training and tens of thousands of dollars spent, the summit right there — "just thirty more minutes" feels irresistible. In 1996, climbers on Everest ignored their turnaround times. They summited late. They descended in darkness, into a storm. Some of them never descended at all.

The turnaround time is tonight's central machine: a decision made by the smartest version of you, handed forward to the most compromised version of you — with no renegotiation allowed. Because execution, friend, is where the four defaults come back for revenge.
Kill the plan before it kills you
Before you execute at all, there's a stress test most rooms never run. The usual version — "does anyone see any problems?" — dies under optimism and social pressure.

Pause and guess: Psychologist Gary Klein designed a version that changes ONE thing about the question — and research found it boosts people's ability to correctly identify causes of outcomes by roughly 30 percent. What's the change?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Announce that the project has ALREADY failed — completely — and ask everyone to explain why. That's the premortem, friend, and the shift from "might fail" to "has failed" is not cosmetic: research on prospective hindsight found that imagining an event as having already occurred unlocks specificity — "we failed" prompts concrete causes (the supplier flaked, the timeline assumed nobody got sick, our champion left the company) where "we might fail" prompts vague hedging. Certainty unlocks specificity. And it fixes a social problem too: in a normal meeting, the skeptic looks disloyal; in a premortem, finding failure modes is the assignment — the most junior voice can raise what everyone privately fears. Run it in three steps: state the frame (one year from now, this was a disaster); have everyone generate reasons independently — before discussion anchors the room; then patch the plan — eliminate the preventable, buffer the unavoidable, convert the rest into monitoring signals. A plan that has survived its own imagined autopsy, friend, fails less often — and fails smaller. Then arm the tripwires: a bright-line signal you can't argue with (a date, a dollar figure, a metric — "if we haven't hit 100 paying users by March 1, we shut it down") plus a pre-committed response. "We'll revisit if things get bad" is not a tripwire — vagueness invites exactly the rationalization it was meant to prevent. And the strongest version ties your hands entirely: give a colleague standing authority to enforce it, because your future self will lobby against the rule. Design the rule so the lobbying fails.

One more execution tool, borrowed from the military: commander's intent. No plan survives contact with reality, and you can't be everywhere the plan meets it — so communicate the objective and the why, not a fragile chain of steps. Everyone executing your decision should answer two questions without calling you: what outcome are we actually trying to achieve — and why? Then, when the supplier misses the shipment, the person who knows only their task list stalls; the person who knows the intent adapts on the spot — and usually correctly. And note the discipline it forces on you, friend: if you can't state the intent in a few sentences... you haven't finished deciding.
The most dangerous quadrant

Now the deepest idea in the whole decision section — the one poker players guard like a trade secret. Decision quality and outcome quality are different things, linked only loosely, because luck sits between them. The drunk driver who arrives home safely did not make a good decision. The well-reasoned bet that loses was not a mistake.

Pause and guess: Draw the two-by-two: good/bad process against good/bad outcome. Three of the four squares teach honest lessons. One is a trap that poker players call the most dangerous square on the board. Which one — and why?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Bad process, good outcome — dumb luck disguised as skill. Earned success (good/good) — repeat it. Bad luck (good process, bad outcome) — repeat the process anyway. Bad/bad is at least an honest teacher. But the lucky win, friend, reinforces exactly the behavior most likely to ruin you later — and judging by results alone, what poker players call resulting, teaches systematically wrong lessons: reward the reckless bet that paid off, and you train yourself and your whole organization to take more reckless bets... right up until variance collects. Punish the sound decision that got unlucky, and people stop making sound decisions and start managing appearances. Over time, outcome-only judgment selects for gamblers and politicians rather than thinkers. The practical conclusion flows from what you control: you do not control outcomes — you control only the process — how you defined the problem, what options you generated, what criteria and safeguards you built. And process, unlike luck, compounds: each well-made decision leaves you in a better position, and position — the book's opening argument, now complete — determines your future options. Judge yourself and your people on the process visible at the time of the decision, friend, and let outcomes be data about the world — never verdicts on your worth.

But there's a saboteur between you and that discipline: hindsight bias — the "I knew it all along" effect that quietly rewrites memory until whatever happened seems obvious. Uncertainty you genuinely felt disappears; lucky guesses become foresight. You cannot learn from experience that keeps getting edited. The countermeasure is the decision journal: at the moment of choice — before any results exist — write the situation, the variables, what you decided, the alternatives you rejected, your expectations with rough probabilities... and how you feel, physically and mentally — because tired, rushed, and angry leave fingerprints on decisions, and the journal is how you learn to spot yours. When outcomes arrive, the entry answers what resulting never can: good decision, or just good outcome? Over dozens of entries, patterns surface that no single decision reveals — the domains where you're overconfident, the moods that correlate with your worst calls. Written honestly and at the time, friend, your own history becomes your training set.
Before you go

So: the turnaround time is a decision mailed forward from your clearest self to your most compromised one; the premortem's fake certainty surfaces real risks, and tripwires make the exit automatic; commander's intent delegates the goal, not the steps; luck divorces outcomes from decisions, and the lucky win is the most dangerous square on the board; and the decision journal is the only honest witness against your own rewriting memory. This week, friend: attach one bright-line tripwire to the bet you're most emotionally invested in — and tell someone, so you can't quietly renegotiate.

One night remains in this book — and it asks the question hiding under all the others, friend. You can define problems brilliantly, weigh options like an investor, execute like a field commander... and still spend your one life winning games that were never worth playing. Tomorrow, the finale: what the dying regret, what the successful get wrong, and how to want what actually matters. Next time: the hidden lesson.
Key takeaways
Execution is where the defaults return: decide the turnaround time in the valley, not on the ridge — 1996 Everest is the tuition.
Premortem: "it already failed — why?" beats "what might go wrong?" by ~30% — certainty unlocks specificity, and skepticism becomes the assignment.
Tripwires need a bright-line signal plus a pre-committed response — and an enforcer outside your emotional blast radius.
Commander's intent: delegate the outcome and the why; if you can't state the intent in two sentences, you haven't finished deciding.
Never "result": good process/bad outcome is bad luck; bad process/good outcome is the trap that ruins you later.
Keep a decision journal at the moment of choice — it's the only defense against hindsight bias, and your history becomes your training set.
